detail.title: Spatial Dependence and Neighbourhood Effect: Explaining Economics, Politics, and Society across the World

declarations.ethicsApproval: I have a consent to publish this paper. I declare no conflict of interests

keywords: neighbourhood effect. Research area: social sciences

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Siberian Federal University. Humanities & Social Sciences 2023 16(9): 1616–1629

detail.abstract: In this paper the authors present the results of a large-scale study that proposes a holistic approach to assess spatial distribution of various social phenomena across the world. 70 statistical indicators describing the political, economic, military, sociodemographic and ideological and value factors that determine the structure of modern international relations were selected and underwent a set of spatial econometrics procedures. For this purpose, such methodological instruments were chosen as dasymetric mapping, geographical anamorphosis, Moran's I, local indicators of spatial association clustering (LISA) and multidimensional scaling. The authors illustrate each step with an overview of the obtained results for all or certain indicators, for instance, those which demonstrated statistically significant LISA clustering results for the Balkan countries. Furthermore, the authors proposed Spatial Dependence Index (SDI) to identify where the spatial influence is identified separately from other factors on the examples of such statistical indicators as GDP PPP per capita, religiosity level, suicide rates, etc. The conducted research was aimed to test the methods of spatial econometrics to the political map of the world, it shows a set of tools capable of explaining the changing structure of world politics and revealing the transformations of local clusters in different regions of the world. The authors conclude that the proposed spatial econometrics approach is holistic and helps to identify and interpret state behaviour patterns and, in broad sense, social phenomena through the geographical lens. The findings from this study support the use of GeoDA software and make a significant contribution to understanding the degree of space influence on phenomena distribution and international relations in general.

title: Believed Gender Differences in Parenting Attitudes and Labor Supply
affiliations: and University of Nottingham - School of Economics

detail.title: Believed Gender Differences in Parenting Attitudes and Labor Supply
detail.abstract: We study whether beliefs about gendered parenting sustain "second-hurdle" child penalties at school age. In a large-scale online survey of U.S. parents, respondents evaluated vignettes that present symmetrically positioned dual-earner parents and reported beliefs about three parenting traits: effectiveness, enjoyment, and willingness. Despite symmetry, 76% recommend mothers reduce work and advise larger hour cuts for mothers. Only perceived gendered willingness to sacrifice time predicts these gendered recommendations; perceived effectiveness or enjoyment do not. Endorsing the traditional family roles strengthens the gap. A randomized video treatment highlighting a career-focused mother leaves recommendations unchanged but increases blaming mothers for child's poor performance.

title: Causal-Text: An Interpretable Framework for Causal Inference with Text
affiliations: Tsinghua University and Tsinghua University

detail.title: Causal-Text: An Interpretable Framework for Causal Inference with Text
detail.abstract: Natural language processing has made significant strides, yet its application in causal inference remains challenging due to the high-dimensional nature of text. This often leads to biased estimations from confounding variables hidden within the text. In this paper, we introduce Causal-Text, a novel and interpretable framework to rigorously incorporate unstructured text into causal inference with structured data. Our framework consists of three main stages: (1) We use a pre-trained language model (BERT) to construct a correlation matrix between the text and other variables, proving its theoretical soundness. (2) We apply causal discovery algorithms to this matrix to recover the underlying causal structure and identify a sufficient adjustment set, a step often overlooked in prior work. (3) We estimate the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) using a propensity score-based method, leveraging the fine-tuned BERT for more accurate predictions. We conduct extensive experiments on two real-world datasets, PeerRead and Yelp, demonstrating that our framework effectively reduces estimation bias compared to existing methods. The results underscore the necessity of the causal discovery step and highlight the advantages of Causal-Text in terms of interpretability and completeness.

title: A Unified Framework for Spatial and Temporal Treatment Effect Boundaries: Theory and Identification
affiliations: University of Tokyo

detail.title: A Unified Framework for Spatial and Temporal Treatment Effect Boundaries: Theory and Identification
detail.abstract: This paper develops a unified theoretical framework for detecting and estimating boundaries in treatment effects across both spatial and temporal dimensions. We formalize the concept of treatment effect boundaries as structural parameters characterizing regime transitions where causal effects cease to operate. Building on reaction-diffusion models of information propagation, we establish conditions under which spatial and temporal boundaries share common dynamics governed by diffusion parameters $(\delta, \lambda)$, yielding the testable prediction $d^*/\tau^* = 3.32\lambda\sqrt{\delta}$ for standard detection thresholds. We derive formal identification results under staggered treatment adoption and develop a three-stage estimation procedure implementable with standard panel data. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate excellent finite-sample performance, with boundary estimates achieving RMSE below 10\% in realistic configurations. We apply the framework to two empirical settings: EU broadband diffusion (2006-2021) and US wildfire economic impacts (2017-2022). The broadband application reveals a scope limitation—our framework assumes depreciation dynamics and fails when effects exhibit increasing returns through network externalities. The wildfire application provides strong validation: estimated boundaries satisfy $d^* = 198$ km and $\tau^* = 2.7$ years, with the empirical ratio (72.5) exactly matching the theoretical prediction $3.32\lambda\sqrt{\delta} = 72.5$. The framework provides practical tools for detecting when localized treatments become systemic and identifying critical thresholds for policy intervention.

title: AI Unsheathed: Testing Human-AI Collaboration through Deck Construction in Competitive Strategy Games
affiliations: Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD)

detail.title: AI Unsheathed: Testing Human-AI Collaboration through Deck Construction in Competitive Strategy Games
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the role of artificial intelligence as a collaborator in scientific reasoning by framing a known-answer question in the domain of competitive strategy games. Using Flesh and Blood (FaB) and the hero Kassai as a test case, the study evaluates whether AI can navigate both formal constraints and contextual judgment through four hypotheses: metagame identification, mainboard construction, card evaluation, and sideboard design. Results show that while the AI reproduces broad descriptive patterns and aligns well with community consensus, it systematically underestimates dominant strategies, misclassifies card roles, and fails to anticipate dynamic shifts in the competitive environment. Its outputs reflect biases inherited from online sources, revealing limitations in structural reasoning and contextual adaptation. Nonetheless, the AI demonstrates competence in organizing information, synthesizing consensus knowledge, and producing structured outputs. These findings highlight both the promise and the limits of human-AI collaboration: AI can serve as a valuable assistant in knowledge synthesis, but expert oversight remains indispensable to ensure accuracy, contextual awareness, and strategic depth.

title: Common Errors in Equity Valuation: The Misuse of Multiples as a Proxy for Discounted Cash Flow Analysis
affiliations: Columbia University - Columbia Business School

detail.title: Common Errors in Equity Valuation: The Misuse of Multiples as a Proxy for Discounted Cash Flow Analysis

publicationDetails.journalName: Columbia Business School Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Equity valuation is a fundamental aspect of investment decision-making, yet many investors fall into the trap of using short-term multiples, such as price-to-earnings (P/E) or price-to-sales (P/S) ratios, as a proxy for comprehensive discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis. This paper explores the limitations of multiples-based valuation, particularly for growth-oriented firms with significant future cash flows, and we illustrate how reliance on forward multiples can lead to erroneous conclusions about a company's intrinsic value. We further advocate for DCF as the preferred method for capturing long-term value and highlight the risks of superficial valuation practices, especially in the context of social media-driven investment narratives. Our findings underscore the need for rigorous, forward-looking analysis to avoid mispricing opportunities.

title: The New Vaccine Federalism in the U.S.
affiliations: Villanova University - Charles Widger School of Law and

detail.title: The New Vaccine Federalism in the U.S.

detail.abstract: U.S. vaccine policy is rapidly changing—and increasingly pitting federal and state vaccine regulators against one another. Most recently, states on both coasts have formed regional networks with the explicit purpose of countering federal guidelines in the vaccine space.  These recent events present new challenges for vaccine federalism, as well as for public health federalism in general. We contrast the differences between the traditional model of vaccine federalism and the emerging paradigms introduced by the ongoing shifts in vaccine policy. We then consider the long-term implications of the intensifying rift between federal and state vaccine regulators.

detail.abstract: This report outlines findings from King’s College London Legal Clinic and the King’s Policy Institute, following their London-based investigation into local authority refusals to see homeless applicants face to face. The report finds that many local authorities now require online or phone applications and will not initially see homeless applicants in person. It outlines the impact these practices have on people experiencing homelessness, who turn to the healthcare sector for support, in particular hospital emergency departments. The impact on hospitals is also considered, along with some practical and policy recommendations.

title: Agglomerations, Urbanization and Economic Prosperity in Pakistan: A Demographic Analysis Using Ardl Approach for Time Series Data
affiliations: and Government College University Lahore (GCUL)

detail.title: Agglomerations, Urbanization and Economic Prosperity in Pakistan: A Demographic Analysis Using Ardl Approach for Time Series Data
detail.abstract: The current study aims to explore the relationship between agglomerations, urbanization and economic prosperity in Pakistan. The empirical analysis is based on secondary dataset i.e. World Development Indicators and Autoregressive Distribute Lag Model (ARDL) has been applied for the time period 1960-2016. The findings depicts that in the long run agglomeration economies are contributing positively more to economic prosperity compared to the share of overall urban population. However in the short run the effect of the latter variable is found negative. All these results suggest that the governments should focus on policies specifically related to the infrastructure building and the provision of basic services in the cities to improve the process of urbanization. This is the only way to increase the agglomerations in the economy and its outcome in the form of generating more economies of scale.

title: ViTranCoC: Vision Transformers and Conformal Calibration for Industrial Anomaly Detection
affiliations: University of Douala, University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC) - School of Computer Science and Engineering and University of Electronic Science and Technology of China (UESTC)

detail.title: ViTranCoC: Vision Transformers and Conformal Calibration for Industrial Anomaly Detection
detail.abstract: Industrial anomaly detection requires identifying defective products using exclusively nominal training samples, a constraint known as cold-start or one-class classification. Current memory-based approaches employing convolutional neural networks exhibit biases toward ImageNet classification tasks and rely on heuristic threshold selection methods. This paper presents ViTranCoC, a framework that employs Vision Transformers with self-supervised DINO pretraining to extract patch-level representations from industrial images. The proposed method introduces three technical contributions. First, Vision Transformer architectures are adapted to extract multi-scale patch features that capture local defect patterns and global structural anomalies while avoiding classification bias from supervised pretraining. Second, a deformable self-similarity pooling mechanism adjusts receptive fields based on local patch content, enhancing feature discriminability while preserving spatial coherence. Third, splitconformal calibration provides statistical guarantees on anomaly detection thresholds through a mathematically grounded procedure with theoretical coverage bounds. Experiments on the MVTec Anomaly Detection benchmark demonstrate that ViTran-CoC achieves 99.43% image-level AUROC with 95% confidence intervals of [99.12%, 99.68%], exceeding the previous stateof-the-art of 95.3% by 4.13 percentage points while providing calibrated uncertainty estimates. Evaluation on Magnetic Tile Defects (98.87% AUROC) and mini ShanghaiTech Campus (94.72% pixel-wise AUROC) datasets confirms generalization across industrial inspection and surveillance applications without domain-specific adaptation.

title: Brief of Amici Curiae in Support of the Petitioner for Rehearing En Banc; Ass'n. of New Jersey Rifle and Pistol Clubs, Inc., et al., v. Attorney General New Jersey, 974 F.3d 237 (3rd Cir. 2020).
affiliations: FPC Action Foundation, University of Wyoming - Firearms Research Center and University of Wyoming College of Law

detail.title: Brief of Amici Curiae in Support of the Petitioner for Rehearing En Banc; Ass'n. of New Jersey Rifle and Pistol Clubs, Inc., et al., v. Attorney General New Jersey, 974 F.3d 237 (3rd Cir. 2020).
detail.abstract:
The first known repeating arms, which fired 10 consecutive shots, date to between 1490 and 1530. A 1580 firearm could fire 16 shots.

In the 17th century, two European repeater models were widely copied and produced, including in the American colonies: Denmark’s 30-round Kalthoff long gun, and Italy’s 7-round Lorenzoni handgun.

Other repeaters were being manufactured in the colonies by the mid-1600s. Repeaters capable of firing more than 10 rounds gained popularity by the early 1700s. During the Revolutionary War, the Continental Congress ordered repeaters that could “discharge sixteen, or twenty [rounds], in sixteen, ten, or five seconds.”

The state-of-the-art rifle when the Second Amendment was ratified had a 22-round magazine. Meriwether Lewis acquired one from a Pennsylvania gunsmith and carried it on the Lewis and Clark Expedition, frequently demonstrating it to prove that his small party could defend itself even if outnumbered. America’s Founders knew about and embraced such arms.

Repeaters with greater than 10-round capacities became some of the 19th century’s most popular arms—including the iconic Winchester and Henry rifles, followed by semiautomatic repeaters after 1885.

In the 20th century, the federal government supplied American citizens with nearly a quarter-million arms with 15- and 30-round magazines through the Civilian Marksmanship Program, in addition to numerous 30-round magazines the program issued independently of firearms. American history and tradition prove that the Second Amendment protects such arms.

title: Bankability And Contract Enforcement In Nigerian Public-Private Partnerships: The Role Of Security Interests, Collateral Arrangements, Risk Allocation And Lender Protections In Infrastructure Transactions
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Bankability And Contract Enforcement In Nigerian Public-Private Partnerships: The Role Of Security Interests, Collateral Arrangements, Risk Allocation And Lender Protections In Infrastructure Transactions
detail.abstract: Public-private partnerships (PPPs) are simply ways through which Nigeria can put up with critical infrastructure in regions where the government is unable to carry out allocation of sufficient funding, like transportation, healthcare and energy. For these partnerships to record success in their activities, it is essential that they are structured in a manner that would entice private investors to participate. This is primarily due to the fact that investors are interested in ensuring that projects will be successful and that promises will be fulfilled. Notwithstanding these, some investors are often not inclined to really invest in Nigerian PPPs. This is due to the absence of confidence in the institutions, the law, and/or even the potential for frequent political interference. These problems make it really difficult for PPPs to secure long-term financing. As a result of this, lenders are only able to provide funding to PPPs when they are confident that the risks are or would be shared equitably, that money will be repaid and that the PPPs will also fulfill their own obligations. The Nigeria’s experience shows that these guarantees are affected by delay in dispute resolution, inconsistencies in regulatory frameworks, and inadequate legal safeguards. As a result of this, projects and initiatives that have potentials to cause economic growth often encounter difficulties in attaining financial stability and closure, thereby necessitating the essence of an effective legal and contractual framework to drive investor confidence.

title: Branding WQĀF for Sustainable Development: A Marketing Approach
affiliations: Bayero University Kano - Department of Economics

detail.title: Branding WQĀF for Sustainable Development: A Marketing Approach

declarations.funderStatement: There was no external funding for the work.

detail.abstract: Recent years have seen discussions on the need to develop the managerial architecture of wqāf to align it with modern realities. Awqāf are suffering from a lack of funds to run their activities. The image of some awqāf has been damaged by poor performance, historical neglect, and colonial past. Efforts at redeveloping wqāf must not neglect organizational image building. To achieve this, the use of modern marketing and communication tools is inevitable. The focus of this paper, therefore, is not on defining wqāf or describing its functions but on creating a good image of wqāf in the public mind. The role of organization's image in the public mind in helping the organization achieve its mission has long been recognized by marketing and communication scholars. Hence the research method followed for this work is an intensive study of selected literature and a critical analysis of their contents. The work also benefits from careful study of existing awqāf operations. Thus, this work is conceptual in nature. It is observed that wqāf shall provide the needed resources for dealing with long-term challenges that require painstaking efforts going beyond political winds and short-term business interests. These include supporting efforts at tackling environmental challenges such as afforestation campaigns and green financing.

title: When Economic Performance Turns on the Colonized Rather than the Colonist
affiliations: Harvard Law School

detail.title: When Economic Performance Turns on the Colonized Rather than the Colonist
detail.abstract: Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson posit that colonizing countries promoted growth in places where their citizens planned to live by introducing rational economic and legal institutions. By contrast, where they faced high mortality rates, they introduced only "extractive" institutions. They took what they could and left. The former places thrived; the latter failed. Disproportionately, Acemoglu, et al.'s countries with high settler mortality rates were places that had only recently made the transition from hunter-gatherer economies to settled agriculture, if they had made it at all. Unlike agriculturalists, hunter-gatherers generally lack any sense of private ownership over the most obvious capital asset-land. Not owning that capital asset, they have little reason to defer gratification and invest in it. And for the most part, they relentlessly fight each other over resources and women. With no tradition of capital ownership or long-term investments but with chronic and lethal violence, most hunter-gatherers would not have been able effectively to exploit rational legal institutions anyway. I illustrate (only illustrate; I do not claim to prove) this intuition with the example of the Japanese Ainu. As of the mid-19th century, most Japanese lived either in settled agricultural communities or in booming commercial cities. The hunter-gatherer Ainu, however, lived in the northern-most island of Hokkaido. When the Japanese government introduced western legal institutions at the turn of the century, it applied the new rules both to the agricultural and commercial regions outside of Hokkaido and to the hunter-gatherer communities within Hokkaido. Over most of Japan, men and women quickly learned to exploit the opportunities presented by the new legal system. In Hokkaido, the Ainu failed to do any of that. In time, they simply intermarried with the other Japanese and disappeared. The innovation and investment that would eventually transform Hokkaido came instead with immigrants from the rest of Japan.

title: The Sustainability-Adjusted Valuation Model (SAVM): Extending Discounted Cash Flow for ESG and Climate Risk.

detail.title: The Sustainability-Adjusted Valuation Model (SAVM): Extending Discounted Cash Flow for ESG and Climate Risk.
detail.abstract: The canonical Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) model remains the dominant framework for corporate and investment valuation, yet its reliance on purely financial parameters limits its ability to capture the material effects of environmental, social, and governance (ESG) factors and climate-related risks. This paper introduces the Sustainability-Adjusted Valuation Model (SAVM), a conceptual extension of DCF that explicitly integrates sustainability considerations into both projected cash flows and discount rates. By embedding ESG performance, regulatory transition pathways, physical climate risk, and stakeholder externalities within a systematic valuation equation, SAVM aligns financial analysis with the realities of sustainable business performance. The model is situated within established disclosure and risk frameworks such as the Task Force on Climate-related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) and the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS), and it offers a structured methodology for scenario analysis under varying climate and policy futures. SAVM aims to advance the literature on sustainable finance by providing a unified mathematical and conceptual tool for corporate managers, investors, and policymakers seeking to reconcile longterm value creation with ESG and climate imperatives.

title: Price and Output Elasticities of Industrial Energy Demand in New EU Member States​

detail.title: Price and Output Elasticities of Industrial Energy Demand in New EU Member States​
detail.abstract: We analyse the determinants of industrial energy demand in five new European Union member states (Czechia, Lithuania, Poland, Romania, and Slovenia) with a focus on the effects of energy prices, sectoral output, energy-saving investment, and technological progress. Using a panel dataset covering 16 industrial sectors over more than two decades (1995-2018), we employ advanced estimation approaches commonly used in the related literature to address issues of heterogeneity, cross-sectional dependence, and persistence, often overlooked in studies relying solely on fixed effects. Our empirical results show that output levels and energy prices consistently influence energy consumption, with their effects amplified when cross-correlations are taken into account. From our preferred estimation procedure (Dynamic Common Correlated Effects - Mean Group), we obtain evidence of intuitively relevant values: the energy price elasticity is -0.42, and the output elasticity is 0.32. Energy demand exhibits moderate levels of persistence, showing that past consumption patterns drive current energy consumption. Energy-saving investments tend to increase energy use, as they often accompany industrial growth or modernisation, whereas research and development show only a limited effect. These findings provide policymakers with valuable insights into energy solutions that can influence energy demand and mitigate the pressures of industrial growth.

title: Fuel taxes without borders: Causal evidence on diesel and gasoline demand in the European Union
affiliations: University of Ljubljana School of Economics and Business

detail.title: Fuel taxes without borders: Causal evidence on diesel and gasoline demand in the European Union
detail.abstract: This paper quantifies the causal effects of retail fuel prices and cross-border price differentials on national road-fuel demand in the European Union, using harmonized monthly panel data for 24 countries from 2008 to 2024. We exploit exogenous variation in retail prices induced by national excise tax changes, instrumenting for endogeneity with statutory tax rates, and estimate two-stage least squares (2SLS) models with country and month fixed effects, clustering standard errors at the country level. For diesel, we find a robust own-price elasticity of −1.82, indicating that a 10% increase in the retail price reduces domestic consumption by 18%. The price gap with neighbouring countries is also significant: a 10% increase in the neighbour-relative price reduces domestic demand by 8.3%. A dyadic IV model, which directly instruments the neighbour–home price difference, yields a cross-border elasticity of −0.52, consistent with substantial cross-border substitution. For gasoline, the own-price elasticity is small and statistically insignificant (−0.14), but the dyadic IV model reveals a significant cross-border elasticity of −0.41, indicating that cross-border fuel tourism is a key adjustment margin for gasoline. The stronger price sensitivity for diesel likely reflects the dominance of commercial road freight, which is more responsive to price incentives and tax-driven arbitrage than private gasoline use. These findings highlight the importance of coordinated tax policy in integrated markets, as uncoordinated national tax hikes can trigger significant cross-border fuel shopping, undermining both revenue and environmental goals.

title: Designing Informational Environments in Online Learning: Career-Prospect Information, Guided Discovery, and Self-Determination
affiliations: , Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business, Arizona State University and Arizona State University (ASU) - W.P. Carey School of Business

detail.title: Designing Informational Environments in Online Learning: Career-Prospect Information, Guided Discovery, and Self-Determination
detail.abstract: Rapid technological change and labor market disruption have made continuous reskilling a critical imperative, with technology-mediated environment such as MOOCs emerging as key vehicles for acquiring IT-related skills. However, sustaining self-regulated learning (SRL) in these environments remains a persistent challenge. While prior IS research emphasizes interventions such as gamification, little is known about whether-and how-career-relevant labor market information influences learner motivation and outcomes. Grounded in the Interactive, Constructive, Active, and Passive (ICAP) framework, we theorize that the format of information delivery conditions the internalization of career-prospect cues and the self-determination that drives increased learning effort and performance. We test our theory in a field experiment within an undergraduate online certificate program in business data analytics, randomly assigning students to a control, passive information reception, or guided discovery conditions. Results show that while both treatments increase surface-level engagement, only guided discovery improves assignment performance, spillover course participation, and intentions to pursue further education. Mechanism analyses reveal that guided discovery reduces personal belief error and is most effective among students who initially underestimated their career prospects or displayed stronger self-regulated learning ability. These patterns illustrate a self-determination mechanism, whereby guided discovery enables learners to autonomously internalize labor market signals and view them as personally attainable goals. Our findings extend IS research on technology-mediated learning by identifying informational environments as a distinct design dimension of educational IT artifacts and by showing how information presentation format drives internalization and self-determined motivation.

title: Hybrid Neuro-Fuzzy System for Energy Demand Forecasting: A Soft Computing Approach
affiliations: World Citi Colleges, Universidad De Manila, World Citi Colleges, Lyceum of Tingloy de San Roque Inc and Lyceum of Tingloy de San Roque Inc

detail.title: Hybrid Neuro-Fuzzy System for Energy Demand Forecasting: A Soft Computing Approach

declarations.ethicsApproval: This study, titled “Hybrid Neuro-Fuzzy System for Energy Demand Forecasting: A Soft Computing Approach,” did not involve human participants, patients, or animals. The research utilized publicly available secondary data obtained from the Philippine Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC) covering the years 2018–2023. As such, formal ethics approval was not required. However, all data were handled in compliance with ethical research standards, ensuring confidentiality, responsible data use, and adherence to institutional and national research ethics guidelines.

detail.abstract: The Philippine energy sector faces growing challenges from rising electricity demand, rapid renewable integration, and weather-driven variability, requiring more accurate and adaptive forecasting methods. This study presents a hybrid neuro-fuzzy system (HNFS) for short-term energy demand forecasting, leveraging the learning capacity of neural networks and the interpretability of fuzzy logic to address the nonlinearity and uncertainty inherent in power consumption patterns. Using hourly electricity and weather data from the Philippine Energy Regulatory Commission (2018-2023), the model employed k-nearest-neighbor imputation, normalization, and mutual information-based feature selection. The HNFS integrates a three-layer feedforward network with adaptive fuzzy inference and was trained on a 70/15/15 train-validation-test split. Results show superior accuracy over ARIMA and LSTM baselines, achieving a MAPE of 3.9% and RMSE of 14.6 MW-representing a 55% improvement in RMSE compared to ARIMA and a 31% improvement compared to LSTM. Key advantages include dynamic adaptation to seasonal variability, faster convergence, and transparent fuzzy rules that enhance interpretability. These capabilities enable improved grid stability, facilitate renewable energy integration, and support policy development for demand-side management. The findings demonstrate that soft computing, through HNFS, provides a robust and explainable framework that can be deployed in smart grid operations and real-time energy management across the Philippines.

title: Patent or Planet? Rethinking IP for Just Climate Tech Transition in the Global South
affiliations: TC Beirne School of Law, University of Queensland

detail.title: Patent or Planet? Rethinking IP for Just Climate Tech Transition in the Global South
detail.abstract: Equitable technology transfer is a cornerstone of achieving a just transition (JT), enabling climate resilience and sustainable development in the Global South. While intellectual property (IP) protections are designed to incentivize innovation, they often constrain access to climate technologies, creating systemic barriers for nations in the Global South. Through a dual lens of doctrinal and qualitative analysis, this article examines the contested role of IP systems (particularly the World Trade Organization's TRIPS and TRIPS-plus clauses in trade agreements) in shaping the global landscape of climate technology transfer. It highlights the implications for achieving a JT and the geopolitical asymmetries that perpetuate technological dependency, and the potential pathways for strengthening Southern agency. Findings reveal that current IP frameworks exacerbate inequities but also highlight actionable reforms. The article calls for reimagining IP governance as an instrument for equity and climate justice, urging international collaboration to dismantle colonial legacies embedded in global knowledge systems and advance innovation through commons-based approaches essential for sustainable futures.

title: Consumer Response to Silent Branding in High End Fashion
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Consumer Response to Silent Branding in High End Fashion
detail.abstract: This study investigates Indian consumers' preferences for silent branding, characterized by understated craftsmanship, elegance, and exclusivity, within India's fashion landscape. It examines the influence of social media on the accessibility and consumption patterns of silent branding. A quantitative approach was employed, utilizing an online survey with a self-structured questionnaire based on a 5-point Likert scale, administered to consumers in Tier 1 and Tier 2 Indian cities via random sampling, complemented by literature review. The findings indicate a growing consumer inclination towards silent branding in India, driven by aspirations for sustainability, sophistication, and cultural diversity. Social media plays a significant role in democratizing access to silent luxury brands through curated content, influencer marketing, and online marketplaces, thereby improving discovery. However, platforms like Pinterest and Instagram have paradoxically made silent branding "less silent" due to intensified demand from influencer marketing and viral trends, potentially diluting its subtle appeal. The study highlights the inherent tension between exclusivity and accessibility in the current market, offering insights for brands navigating this shift. Marketers face the challenge of balancing broad reach with maintaining the core ethos of silent branding while utilizing social media to engage aspirational consumers. These insights contribute to broader discussions on online influence, consumer behavior, and the evolving definition of luxury in India's high-end fashion sector.

title: Short-Term Pain for Long-Term Gain: Adaptive Experiment with Post-Commitment Reward Shift
affiliations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management and Chinese University of Hong Kong

detail.title: Short-Term Pain for Long-Term Gain: Adaptive Experiment with Post-Commitment Reward Shift
detail.abstract: Due to state-level actions and geopolitical tensions, more and more practitioners are impacted by anticipated business environment shifts, including new data privacy rules, environmental regulations, tariffs, restricted access to key production components, etc. To address those challenges, companies are proactively exploring substitute operational plans for long-term resilience. However, companies in such exploration environments face a dilemma when their short-term optimal actions may not favor their long-term benefits. To understand the fundamental tradeoff behind the dilemma and provide rule of thumb to guide decision-makers’ experiment design, we consider an adaptive experiment with post-commitment reward shift problem, which consists of two phases: an experiment phase, where the decision-maker is free to experiment with different options, and a commitment phase, where they must commit to a single option for the remainder of the phase. More importantly, each option’s reward may change after the commitment. Our main result is a simple yet effective algorithm to solve the experimenter’s problem. Our algorithm follows an option-elimination framework, but with special treatments dedicated to dealing with the post-commitment reward shift. We analyze the regret upper bounds of our algorithm across all parameter regimes, and we provide matching lower bounds to illustrate the fundamental tradeoffs. Motivated by specific business practices, we further extend our analysis and results to the setting (1) when the experimenter has prior structural knowledge about the reward shift; (2) when the experimenter has concave rewards in the commitment phase.

detail.abstract: This paper empirically investigates the relationship between President Jair Bolsonaro's public appearances and speeches-delivered without protective measures during the COVID-19 pandemic-and the subsequent increase in infection rates in Brazil. Using a dummy variable equal to one on days of public appearances or speeches and zero otherwise, incorporated into the model with a 14-day lag (corresponding to the average incubation and contagion period), we estimate the impact of these events on the evolution of confirmed cases. The results indicate that the president's public presence and statements significantly contributed to the spread of the virus, highlighting how political communication can influence collective behavior and exacerbate public-health crises.

title: Borrowed Voices, Shared Debt: Plagiarism, Idea Recombination, and the Knowledge Commons in Large Language Models
affiliations: Universidad de la Republica

detail.title: Borrowed Voices, Shared Debt: Plagiarism, Idea Recombination, and the Knowledge Commons in Large Language Models

declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Large language models generate fluent text by recombining the language and ideas of prior authors at scale. This process produces plagiarism-like harms in three dimensions: direct wording leakage, imitation of distinctive styles, and appropriation of argument structures or conceptual syntheses without provenance. At the same time, their capacity to provide insight or novel-seeming combinations depends entirely on the accumulated labor of millions of human writers, editors, teachers, and curators who built the knowledge commons. This paper argues that denunciation and recognition must proceed together: the harms of extraction must be exposed, yet the debt to the commons must also be acknowledged. The article proposes a framework that defines the scope of plagiarism in this context, diagnoses the mechanisms of recombination, and sets out operational remedies, including dataset governance, attribution layers, compensation pools, and measurable audit thresholds. The goal is to establish a system that restricts illegitimate appropriation while reinvesting in the infrastructures of shared knowledge that make such synthesis possible.

detail.abstract:
The interconnected challenges of the 21st-century global economy necessitate a reevaluation of competition law systems worldwide in the spirit of multidisciplinarity. It means not only reviewing in light of its intellectual roots in jurisprudence, microeconomics, and ethics, but also recognizing the rapidly increasing number of valuable insights from contemporary studies on information and complexity. title: Integrity Leadership and Sustainable Management Practices for Nigeria's Sustainability
affiliations: Rhema Univeristy, Nigeria.

detail.title: Integrity Leadership and Sustainable Management Practices for Nigeria's Sustainability
detail.abstract: Leading and managing are concepts that dominate development and sustainability literature because of their pivotal roles in resource allocation and control. Since the early postulation that leadership is the ability to influence and inspire others and goes with coercive power, expert power, referent power, and others, it is very likely that no serious thought has been given to the relationship of leadership and integrity. Integrity emphasizes a condition of honesty or selflessness which is crucial for doing the right thing. Integrity leadership manifests in unshakeable honesty and a splendid behavior in the interaction of the leader and the follower. It opens the way for people to be helpful, encouraging, and genuinely interested in other people, demonstrating generosity, being considerate of others feelings, developing a good sense of honour and ultimately providing selfless service to others and society. Integrity leadership then becomes the driver of sustainable management practices required for the efficient management of a country's vast resource wealth like oil and gas, material, human and financial resources often wasted through manipulative leadership and unsustainable management practices in many countries. The concept of integrity leadership has the huge potential to foster trust as a cornerstone for service and honour. Integrity leadership is not about charismatic or democratic leadership, but a unique compass for passing the tests of ethics, fairness, truth, justness, equality, selflessness and candor. In a deep reflection of the classic selfless leadership of Nelson Mandela, integrity leadership presents a practical walking encyclopedia of transparency, accountability, decency, humility and honour as ingredients for sustainability. This would immediately suggest that integrity leadership is not only critical to combating corruption and promoting sustainable governance but it also relates to restoring trust and confidence in democratic politics and ethical standards. The investigation literature review research design was adopted for this study and the result showed significant positive relationship between integrity leadership and Nigeria's sustainability. The study was not exhaustive due to lack of current relevant literature and research funding. Further study could examine the relationship between democratic leadership and public sector fraud because of the massive fraud unfolding in the Nigerian public sector. The study recommends that sustainability is a function of integrity and people appointed to lead or management must be people of proven integrity and not those brandishing certificates without morality or integrity.

title: The Fiscal Health of Michigan Local Governments 2023
affiliations: University of Michigan at Ann Arbor - Gerald R. Ford School of Public Policy, University of Michigan at Ann Arbor and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor - Gerald R. Ford School of Public Policy

detail.title: The Fiscal Health of Michigan Local Governments 2023
detail.abstract: This report provides an annual update on Michigan local government fiscal health. Using financial data reported to the State of Michigan in 2023, this analysis develops a set of indicators to look at cash, budgetary, long-term, and service solvency for counties, cities, villages, and townships in Michigan. This update finds that there were few significant changes in overall trends for the fiscal health of Michigan local governments compared to the past few years. Federal aid continues to bolster general fund balances and cash reserves, resulting in strong cash and budgetary solvency measures. However, local governments should beware of “fiscal cliffs” as one-time revenues from pandemic-era aid expire. Local governments continue to show variability in their ability to meet long-term financial and service obligations, due in part to restrictive revenue policy and high long-term liabilities from pensions and retiree healthcare benefits.

title: Transcending Methodological Individualism: A Collectivist Reframing of Remittance Theory in Migration Studies
affiliations: and Leiden University

detail.title: Transcending Methodological Individualism: A Collectivist Reframing of Remittance Theory in Migration Studies

declarations.funderStatement: Research funded by the Leverhulme Trust and the European Research Council

detail.abstract: This paper critiques the use of methodological individualism in remittance theory. Such an approach understands migrants’ transfers as acts of altruism, self-interest, or as reciprocal exchange. We argue for a methodologically collectivist approach which we believe helps highlight the logics and value systems that often underpin remitting practices. This is particularly valid in societies where concepts of kinship, obligation, and shared cultural norms dominate. Drawing on Weber’s distinction between method and values, we show that collectivist analysis is not ideological but analytically productive. Drawing on literature that understands remittances as collectivist practices, we highlight how households and kin networks can operate as decision-making social organisms. Such social organisms reallocate resources across borders to sustain collective well-being. Revisiting the historical political marginalisation of ‘Collectivism’, we call for the term’s reintroduction as an explicit theoretical category to capture the relational, normative, and cultural dimensions of remittances which are often inadequately conceptualised.

title: Information Design for Social Learning with Patient Agents
affiliations: and Shandong University

detail.title: Information Design for Social Learning with Patient Agents
detail.abstract: Sequentially coming agents may adopt a new technology. Early adoption can generate information about its value, which is either high or low, and an intermediary decides how such information will be dynamically published. Because individuals tend to wait and free-ride on information generated by others, efficient social learning is hard to achieve.  Facing this challenge, we study how the intermediary can improve social welfare by designing its information publishing policy. To incentivize early adoption, we show it is optimal to restrain future information flow via inducing individually sub-optimal adoption but not via excessive waiting. The optimal design features a simple threshold stopping structure: in every period, recommend adoption if the intermediary’s current belief is more optimistic than a threshold; otherwise, recommend waiting forever. While the first-best design uses a constant threshold, the optimal design features time-varying thresholds that typically cross the first-best one. We also examine special cases where learning is via conclusive news. In good-news environments, the optimal design needs to involve a middle phase in which exploration is randomly terminated; in bad-news environments, adoption may be continued even if bad news has arrived. These serve to mitigate the individuals’ incentive problem efficiently.

title: Fueling Fluctuations: The Macroeconomic Impact of Energy Price Shocks in Small Open Economies
affiliations: Utrecht University

detail.title: Fueling Fluctuations: The Macroeconomic Impact of Energy Price Shocks in Small Open Economies
detail.abstract: Energy price shocks play a disproportionate role in driving aggregate fluctuations because energy sectors function as hubs in production networks—supplying key inputs to many other central sectors. This hub status allows them to propagate shocks far beyond what their GDP share would suggest. This study quantifies the impact of energy import price shocks on aggregate output in 21 small open European economies, using international sector-level input–output data. I extend the production network framework of Acemoglu, et al. (2012) to a small open economy setting and show that the sensitivity of output to such shocks depends on four structural drivers: (i) the network centrality of primary energy products, (ii) the substitutability between domestic and imported energy, (iii) the pre-shock import–domestic price differential, and (iv) the degree of home bias in energy sourcing. Estimated GDP elasticities with respect to energy import prices range from –0.037 to –0.006 across countries, with differences in network centrality accounting for most of the cross-country variation.

title: The Economics of Unpacked Selling: Strategic Packaging Decisions in Competitive Markets
affiliations: Purdue University - Department of Management and University of Bradford

detail.title: The Economics of Unpacked Selling: Strategic Packaging Decisions in Competitive Markets
detail.abstract: Smart dispenser systems are enabling a resurgence of unpacked selling, where consumers bring reusable containers and purchase products without single-use packaging. Global firms such as Nestlé and Unilever are piloting such models using a variety of technological dispenser machines for coffee, pet food, and detergents, yet the profitability of unpacked selling remains unclear, especially in markets where firms compete in both product quality and packaging format. We develop a game-theoretic model to examine when it is optimal for a firm to offer unpacked products, either in addition to or instead of its packed offerings. Two firms, a high-end and a low-end producer, compete in both content and packaging. Consumers are heterogeneous in how they value sustainability, hygiene, and convenience, which we capture through differentiated packaging valuations. Our results highlight several insights. First, unpacked products require a cost advantage to be viable, but competition changes the thresholds: it raises the bar for introducing unpacked formats while making it easier to eliminate packed formats entirely. Second, firm roles matter: high-end producers are better positioned to guide consumers toward unpacked formats through mixed portfolios, whereas low-end producers are more likely to achieve packaging-free markets. Third, higher consumer valuations may hurt unpacked selling: higher content valuation may shift demand away from low-end unpacked products, and improvements in low-end packaging perception may increase packed sales rather than unpacked sales. Finally, calibration for three exemplar products-coffee, rice, and laundry detergent-demonstrates that our model can replicate observed industry patterns and suggests that reducing unpacked costs alone may be insufficient to eliminate packed formats. Together, these findings provide guidance for firms considering unpacked offerings and for policymakers designing interventions to expand their adoption.

Excerpt

Fundamentals of Operations Strategy: Productivity as a Relative Measure

Productivity Is Relative

Productivity measures are a critical part of understanding, measuring, comparing, and observing changes in a firm's performance over time. In a companion technical note, “Fundamentals of Operations Strategy: Productivity” (UVA-OM-1637), we explained how to calculate productivity measures for Southwest Airlines Co. (Southwest) using data pulled from the 2016 annual report. We calculated the labor productivity as $20.425 billion divided by 43,740 employees to yield a labor productivity of $466,963 revenue per employee. We also calculated equipment productivity by dividing the revenue, $20.425 billion, by the amount of equipment, 723 airplanes, to yield equipment productivity of $28,250,345 revenue per airplane. We can also divide 124,719,765 passengers by 723 airplanes to yield equipment productivity of 172,503 passengers per airplane. In this note, we will move beyond the basic productivity calculations and explore how productivity measurements should be viewed as relative measures.

Let's begin by considering the importance of those previous numbers. Can anything be concluded? Unfortunately, while these values are interesting, they cannot lead to any conclusions in isolation. Obviously, labor and equipment are two very different things, and the productivity measurements associated with each of them are also very different. Comparing labor productivity and equipment productivity is therefore not as useful as comparing similar approaches to calculating productivity. Also, productivity is a relative measure and should be viewed as part of a series or trend, or across similarly calculated productivity measures pertaining to competitors in the same industry. In isolation, or across categories of productivity that are very different, productivity measures are less meaningful.

Benchmarking and Time Series

To make a useful comparison between productivity measures, one must first establish a common basis for comparison. This can be accomplished by either benchmarking, which refers to comparing similar measures for similar companies or for similar business units, or by using a time series, which compares the same measure over time.

title: Towards Virtual Twinning of Mines: Monitoring and Control of Underground Mine Air Quality by Utilising a Parametric 3D BIM Model

detail.title: Towards Virtual Twinning of Mines: Monitoring and Control of Underground Mine Air Quality by Utilising a Parametric 3D BIM Model
detail.abstract: Understanding air quality (AQ) in underground (UG) mine tunnels is vital for ensuring worker health and operational safety. Poor air conditions can pose serious health risks, and regulatory bodies require continuous monitoring and accurate documentation for compliance and inspection. Beyond regulatory needs, comprehensive AQ monitoring enables more effective mitigation of harmful compounds. This study explores the use of three-dimensional information modelling (IM) in UG tunnels to develop a parametric Mine Information Model (MIM). Drawing from Building Information Modelling (BIM) principles established in other sectors, the MIM serves as the basis for a Virtual Twin (VT) that supports AQ visualisation and management of dynamic datasets. The MIM integrates measured and simulated AQ parameters, aligning georeferenced and time-stamped data with a geometric model of the tunnel network. A completely new application of the Large Eddy Simulation (LES) method to simulate AQ in tunnels is also presented. These datasets are then visualised through a VT application, offering real-time environmental insight to support safer daily operations. The system also meets the air monitoring standards outlined in the European Union (EU) Directives on UG environments. Finally, the results and evaluations of a workshop organised among the mine staff to discuss the potential of the new methodology presented in this paper, i.e. information modelling in mining, will be presented.

Fundamentals of Operations Strategy: The Balanced Scorecard

Characteristics of a Balanced Scorecard

This note will explain the concept of a balanced scorecard—what it is, the different elements you would expect in one, and the considerations for its implementation.

A balanced scorecard is a performance-management tool that tracks the execution of activities along a number of dimensions. There are two important things to note. First, tracking the execution of activities is part of operations management, since the operations of a company broadly include all the activities the company performs. Second, a good scorecard uses a number of dimensions, not just one, to track these activities. Including many types of measurements is important because it creates a more complete view of the organization.

A few characteristics are common to all balanced scorecards. First, a balanced scorecard usually focuses on the strategic operations of the organization. Second, a balanced scorecard normally monitors and displays a careful selection of only a small number of metrics. It is not possible to consider monitoring hundreds or thousands of metrics, nor is this approach meaningful from a leadership decision-making perspective. Monitoring a small number of metrics, perhaps only three to five at the most, often makes the most sense. Third, a balanced scorecard normally contains a mix of both financial and nonfinancial metrics.

Bottlenecks and Utilization: Bottlenecks

In this note, we will discuss the concept of a bottleneck, including what it is, some common process terminology associated with bottlenecks, and how to find the bottleneck in any process. The bottleneck is the limiting step in a process. That means it can either be the stage with the lowest capacity or the lowest rate of demand, whichever one is lower. Every process has a bottleneck because every process has a limiting step. As an example, let's look at a three-stage process in which you have already calculated capacity for each stage, and in which you can identify the demand (see Figure 1).

Bottlenecks and Utilization: Resource Utilization

In this note, we will discuss the concept of resource utilization. This material builds on another note in this module, “Bottlenecks and Utilization: Bottlenecks” (UVA-OM-1648), which introduced the concept of the bottleneck. As we discussed in that note, the bottleneck is the stage that limits production and process. Once we know where the bottleneck is, we can understand what the entire process can produce—taking into account the capacity of all process stages working together.

Throughput Rate Is Equal to the Bottleneck

The throughput rate is the rate at which units flow through all process stages working together, expressed as a number of units within a period of time. Returning to the example of a three-stage production process, we see again that the first stage has a capacity of four units per hour, the second stage has a capacity of two units per hour, and the third stage has a capacity of eight units per hour (see Figure 1).

Bottlenecks and Utilization: Capacity 2

In this note, we will further explore capacity calculations. In another technical note in our series of introductory operations management materials, “Current State: Capacity 1” (UVA-OM-1647), we discussed the basic steps for calculating capacity. We examined a two-stage process: Stage one is cutting and stage two is stitching, and there is one worker at each stage (see Figure 1). We calculated the capacity as 10 shirts per week for the cut stage and 20 shirts per week for the stitch stage. We also identified the bottleneck as stage one and calculated the capacity at 10 units per week.

Figure 1. Two-stage process with capacity calculated.

Source: All figures created by authors.

Fewer Workers Than Stages

Now suppose there is only one worker available for both the cut and stitch stages. There are two options in this scenario for calculating capacity. You can either combine the work content of both of the stages (cut, stitch) to reflect the single resource available, or you can determine the amount of time spent on each stage for the single worker. It is also necessary to recalculate the available time, because there is not a full-time worker at each stage; there is only one full-time worker splitting time between each of the two stages.

Product and Process: The Focused Factory

What Is a Focused Factory?

In this note, we will discuss the concept of a focused factory. This includes providing a definition of focused factories and exploring some real-world examples. A focused factory is not necessarily a physical factory that manufactures products. It is a term meant to capture the key operations strategy of a business unit, regardless of whether that business is manufacturing physical products or providing a service. Production is a general set of processes that use resources to transform inputs into outputs of higher value, whether those outputs are goods or services. With that in mind, let's look into the concept of a focused factory.

A focused factory is an operation that strives for a narrow range of processes, products, and intended customers. In other words, it's a specific set of processes designed to create only a few products, which are then intended for consumption by a specific customer group. It's the opposite of “trying to be everything to everyone.” This narrow range allows the operation to focus on doing few things very well, rather than doing many things in a mediocre manner.

Product and Process: Factory Physics

What Are Factory Physics?

In this note, we will define and discuss factory physics and provide details about the levers that are under management control in the factory setting. Factory physics does not actually involve physics. Rather, it is a term meant to capture a key trade-off in manufacturing operations. The word physics is meant to imply the sense of a universal rule that a manager should never forget. That rule has three components:

There is always variability.

The goal of a factory is to match production and demand with the lowest possible cost to produce the highest possible service.

In the context of variability, there are only three buffers available to match production and demand with low cost and high-quality service: inventory, capacity, and lead time.

Fundamentals of Process Improvement:A Brief Background on Process Improvement

A Brief Early History

In this note, we will provide a brief background on process-improvement and quality-management systems. Process improvement is a management philosophy that promotes the continuous improvement of products and services with a strong focus on the involvement of customers and employees. The field of quality management and our modern ideas about quality have emerged over the last 70 to 90 years. In the 1930s and 1940s, early “quality pioneers” W. Edwards Deming, Joseph Juran, and Philip B. Crosby outlined the principles of quality management in several publications.

After World War II, the Japanese (and particularly the executives at Toyota Motor Company) adopted these principles, and Japan held its first national quality award in 1951. However, US and European firms did not begin to implement quality as a branch of management science until the 1980s, when they began to suffer in global markets due to deficits in the relative quality of their products and services. To drive the new initiative home, the United States established the Malcolm Baldrige Quality Award in 1987. Today, quality management is imperative for any business. The bar continues to rise, as competition continues to provide products and services more quickly and cheaply and with more reliability, and to add value to customers in different ways.

title: A Tale of Two Startups: The Loss and Gain of Startups in the U.S. Economy in the Pandemic
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), University of Nevada, Reno - College of Business Administration - Department of Economics and University of Nevada, Reno

detail.title: A Tale of Two Startups: The Loss and Gain of Startups in the U.S. Economy in the Pandemic

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic delivered an unprecedented shock to business entry, with sharply contrasting effects on different types of startups. Using newly constructed administrative data from the Comprehensive Startup Panel covering the universe of U.S. startups, we provide the first official numbers of the pandemics impact on employer and nonemployer startup dynamics. Nonemployer startup formation declined substantially in 2020, while employer startups unexpectedly increased. Survival outcomes also diverged: nonemployer startup survival dropped markedly, whereas employer startup survival remained largely stable. These findings reveal a pronounced compositional shift and underscore the importance of designing policies tailored to nonemployer startups in economic crises.

Fundamentals of Process Improvement:Elements of Process-Improvement Systems

In this note, we will discuss the key elements of a process-improvement system. Process improvement and quality management are more philosophies than specific programs. They bring together continuous process improvement and leadership development, with the customer as the focus of all efforts and improvement activities.

Cultural Alignment and Technical Tools

The first half of a successful quality-improvement program is cultural alignment, which has to do with how leaders respond to and talk about customers. All quality systems and process-improvement programs rely upon a strong leader who is able to define value from the point of view of the customer and communicate that to others. A quality-management program that is not directly linked to customer value as defined by senior leadership and that is not verbally supported by the leader is almost always going to be less successful.

title: A Word of WARN-ing: Advance Notice of Layoffs and Labor Market Outcomes
affiliations: University of Utah - David Eccles School of Business and Washington University in St. Louis

detail.title: A Word of WARN-ing: Advance Notice of Layoffs and Labor Market Outcomes

publicationDetails.journalName: IZA Institute of Labor Economics Discussion Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study investigates the impact of state-level Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification (WARN) Acts on advance notice and post-displacement labor market outcomes for U.S. workers from 1993 to 2019. State WARN adoption increases the likelihood of receiving 30+ days of notice by about 4 percentage points. Instrumental variables estimates, supplemented with local average response functions to address weak instruments, show that lengthy notice reduces immediate joblessness by 4 to 7 percentage points. The effects are most pronounced for low-skill workers. Longer term outcomes are less robust. The results indicate that enforceable mandates improve short run transitions, particularly for vulnerable workers.

Fundamentals of Process Improvement:Tools Used in Process Improvement

In this note, we will discuss some of the key tools used in continuous-improvement systems, also referred to as process-improvement systems. Process flow charts provide an understanding of the inputs and outputs of each process stage, and the motion of material throughout a process. They can help identify where breakdowns occur, how long activities take, and what is most important in terms of receiving items or information from one process stage and providing them to the next process stage.

Run charts are another important process-improvement tool. They help measure the performance of a metric over time, enabling new insights into it. A run chart might record the performance of a metric such as cost or quality over time and is read in a similar way to how one might read a cardiogram.

Scatter diagrams are simple graphs that plot one value against a second value. The first value might be an input to a process stage and the second might be the output. Scatter diagrams help us understand the relationship between two values. They also form the basis of regression analysis and provide insight into how correlated the values are to one another. In other technical notes in this series, we noted that you can perform regression analysis or fit a trend line to data to understand whether the first value is influencing the second one, or if the relationship is reversed.

title: Hired Online: Exploring the Rise of Digital Hiring
affiliations: Sri Sri university, Cuttack

detail.title: Hired Online: Exploring the Rise of Digital Hiring
detail.abstract: This summer internship project report, titled Hired Online: Exploring the Rise of Digital Hiring, conducted at Highland Agro Food Pvt. Ltd., examines the transformative role of digital media in modern talent acquisition. Highland Agro, a leading seafood processing and export company based in Khantapada, Balasore, Odisha, has embraced digital hiring to meet its growing manpower needs. Established in 2022, the company is part of the diversified Highland Group, with a strong focus on quality, sustainability, and innovation. The study investigates how digital platforms, content strategies, and employer branding influence recruitment effectiveness, while comparing digital methods to traditional hiring practices. The research pursued three primary objectives: (1) to explore the role of digital media in contemporary talent acquisition, (2) to analyze how content strategy, platform choice, and employer branding influence recruitment effectiveness, and (3) to evaluate the challenges and opportunities of digital hiring compared to traditional methods. A robust methodology was employed, involving a survey of 40 HR professionals and 100 students/job seekers, conducted over four weeks using Google Forms and structured interviews. Questionnaires included Likert scales, paired-comparison scales, and open-ended questions to capture quantitative and qualitative insights. Data was analyzed using Excel pivot tables, frequency distributions, and cross-tabulations to assess platform usage, candidate preferences, and HR perceptions. Key findings reveal that digital hiring offers significant advantages, including wider reach, cost efficiency, and faster hiring processes, with 72% of candidates recommending online channels for their accessibility. LinkedIn, Indeed, and Naukri emerged as dominant platforms, with 33% of candidates using multi-channel approaches. However, challenges such as digital fatigue, algorithmic biases, and limited digital literacy among rural job seekers persist. Notably, both HR professionals and candidates prioritize human touchpoints, with video interviews and LinkedIn sourcing yielding high satisfaction (75+ score). Highland Agro’s digital hiring efforts are progressing but face gaps in employer branding and platform optimization. Unlike competitors like Thai Union, which excels in digital recruitment through transparent, people-centric content, Highland Agro lacks a robust online presence, with no featured jobs or mission-driven content on platforms like LinkedIn. Recommendations include adopting a hybrid recruitment model, leveraging AI with regular bias audits, and enhancing employer branding through authentic content like “Day-in-the-Life” videos. Strategic partnerships, such as Highland’s MoU with Lulu Group in 2025, further amplify its market potential. By addressing these gaps, Highland Agro can strengthen its talent acquisition strategy and align with global digital hiring trends.

detail.abstract: How much of the most recent surge in inflation expectations, which began in March 2025, has been the result of the usual effect of abnormal price movements? How much is left unexplained and may signal a potential de-anchoring of inflation expectations? How do the most recent and the pandemic-era surges in expectations compare with the two surges in the Great Inflation episode of the 1970s?  This brief addresses those questions using data on inflation expectations from the University of Michigan Survey of Consumers and a simple regression model in which households form their inflation expectations based on their perception of movements in food and gas prices as well as broad-based inflation.
